questions.question: In high-income countries, the epidemiology of TBI has shifted markedly over recent decades. Which mechanism NOW accounts for the largest proportion of moderate-to-severe TBI in this setting?
questions.explanation: In high-income countries, population ageing, frailty, and widespread anticoagulant use have made falls the predominant TBI mechanism, especially among older adults. Road traffic collisions remain the leading cause in low- and middle-income countries.

questions.question: A 38-year-old motorcyclist arrives 90 minutes post-collision with GCS 11, a scalp laceration, and CT showing a small frontoparietal contusion without midline shift. BP is 102/70 mmHg. Which statement regarding tranexamic acid (TXA) is MOST consistent with current evidence?
options: TXA is contraindicated in the presence of intracranial haemorrhage
TXA reduces mortality in mild-to-moderate TBI when given within 3 hours
TXA is only indicated if fibrinogen levels confirm hyperfibrinolysis
TXA should be withheld until a systolic BP >120 mmHg is achieved
TXA shows equivalent mortality benefit in severe isolated TBI (GCS ≤8)
questions.explanation: The CRASH-3 trial demonstrated that TXA reduces head injury-related death in patients with mild-to-moderate TBI (GCS ≥9) when administered within 3 hours of injury. No confirmed coagulopathy is required. TXA is NOT contraindicated by intracranial haemorrhage and shows no clear mortality benefit in severe isolated TBI.

questions.question: A 52-year-old man with severe TBI (GCS 7) following a fall presents with a BP of 88/58 mmHg. Which fluid is MOST appropriate for initial resuscitation?
questions.explanation: 0.9% sodium chloride is the preferred crystalloid for acute TBI resuscitation. Hypotonic solutions (glucose-containing, 0.45% saline) risk cerebral oedema and are contraindicated. Albumin is associated with significantly higher mortality in TBI (SAFE study: 24.6% vs 16%). Balanced crystalloids remain controversial due to their lower sodium content.

questions.question: A patient with severe TBI is haemodynamically unstable (BP 82/50 mmHg) and shows signs of transtentorial herniation (unilateral fixed dilated pupil). Which hyperosmolar agent is PREFERRED?
options: Either agent is equally appropriate; choose by local protocol
Mannitol combined with furosemide to potentiate diuresis
Defer all osmotherapy until blood pressure is normalised
questions.explanation: Hypertonic saline (HTS) is preferred in haemodynamically unstable TBI because it expands intravascular volume and supports blood pressure in addition to reducing ICP. Mannitol causes osmotic diuresis, worsening hypovolaemia and hypotension, and should be avoided in haemodynamically unstable patients.

questions.question: Which intravenous fluid is MOST strongly contraindicated during acute resuscitation in a patient with severe TBI?
options: Packed red blood cells for concurrent haemorrhagic shock
questions.explanation: The SAFE study demonstrated that albumin resuscitation in TBI patients was associated with significantly higher mortality compared with saline (24.6% vs 16%), making albumin the most definitively contraindicated choice. Ringer's lactate is controversial due to slight hypotonicity but lacks the direct RCT mortality evidence that albumin carries.

questions.question: A patient with severe TBI has a mean arterial pressure (MAP) of 88 mmHg and an ICP of 26 mmHg. What is the cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP)?
questions.explanation: CPP = MAP − ICP = 88 − 26 = 62 mmHg. The Brain Trauma Foundation recommends a CPP target of 60–70 mmHg. At 62 mmHg this patient is at the lower end of the acceptable range; ICP-reducing interventions or vasopressor support to raise MAP should be considered.

questions.question: A 29-year-old with severe TBI (GCS 5) suddenly develops a unilateral fixed dilated pupil and extensor posturing. CT is 30 minutes away. Which ventilatory action is MOST appropriate immediately?
options: Increase PEEP to 10 cmH2O to improve oxygenation
Allow PaCO2 to rise above 50 mmHg to maintain cerebral vasodilation
Commence routine hyperventilation targeting PaCO2 28–32 mmHg as standard neuroprotection
Briefly hyperventilate as a temporising bridge to emergency surgery
Maintain current ventilator settings and observe for pupillary recovery
questions.explanation: Brief hyperventilation (hypocapnia → cerebral vasoconstriction → reduced CBF and CBV → decreased ICP) is acceptable as a temporising bridge when impending herniation demands immediate action before surgery. It must NOT be used as a routine or long-term strategy, as sustained hypocapnia risks cerebral ischaemia. PaCO2 should not fall below 30 mmHg even during rescue hyperventilation.

questions.question: Hours after severe TBI, a ventilated patient develops acute pulmonary oedema with hypoxaemia, widespread ST changes on ECG, and markedly elevated troponin. Which mechanism BEST explains these findings?
options: Aspiration pneumonitis from pre-hospital airway compromise
Pre-existing cardiomyopathy decompensated by haemodynamic stress
Catecholamine storm from acute ICP rise causing neurogenic pulmonary oedema
Volume overload from aggressive crystalloid resuscitation in the emergency department
Acute pulmonary embolism from DVT formed at the accident scene
questions.explanation: Neurogenic pulmonary oedema (NPO) and stress-induced cardiomyopathy (Takotsubo-like) in TBI result from a massive catecholamine release driven by acute ICP elevation. This causes increased pulmonary capillary pressure and direct myocardial toxicity. ECG changes and troponin elevation reflect neurogenic cardiac stunning rather than primary coronary disease.

questions.question: A patient with severe TBI requires continuous hypertonic saline infusion for intracranial hypertension. Which serum sodium target range is most commonly recommended to balance ICP reduction against adverse effects?
questions.explanation: A serum sodium target of 145–155 mmol/L is recommended during hyperosmolar therapy with hypertonic saline in TBI. Excessive hypernatraemia (>155 mmol/L) risks renal injury, electrolyte disturbances, and rebound intracranial hypertension. Regular monitoring of sodium and osmolality is mandatory.

questions.question: Regarding intravenous fluid management in acute severe TBI, indicate whether each statement is TRUE or FALSE.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Central venous pressure alone is an adequate endpoint for guiding fluid therapy in TBI

statements.label: B
statements.text: 0.9% sodium chloride is preferred over balanced crystalloids for acute resuscitation in TBI

statements.label: C
statements.text: Albumin resuscitation is associated with improved survival compared with saline in TBI patients

statements.label: D
statements.text: Hypotonic solutions must be avoided as they risk increasing cerebral oedema

questions.explanation: CVP alone is insufficient in TBI — dynamic haemodynamic variables must be integrated. Normal saline is preferred (balanced crystalloids carry possible osmotic harm). The SAFE study showed albumin significantly increased TBI mortality (24.6% vs 16%). Hypotonic fluids lower serum osmolality and must be avoided.

questions.question: Regarding the use of tranexamic acid (TXA) in traumatic brain injury, indicate whether each statement is TRUE or FALSE.

statements.label: A
statements.text: TXA shows clear mortality benefit in severe isolated TBI (GCS ≤8)

statements.label: B
statements.text: Available data confirm a significant increase in thromboembolic events with TXA in TBI patients

statements.label: C
statements.text: TXA should be considered routine therapy for all TBI patients admitted to the ICU regardless of timing or severity

statements.label: D
statements.text: TXA reduces head injury-related mortality in mild-to-moderate TBI when given within 3 hours

questions.explanation: CRASH-3 showed TXA benefit only in mild-to-moderate TBI (GCS ≥9) within 3 hours — not in severe isolated TBI. TXA does not significantly increase thromboembolic events. TXA is NOT routine ICU therapy; its window of efficacy has typically passed by ICU admission.

questions.question: Regarding airway and ventilation management in severe TBI, indicate whether each statement is TRUE or FALSE.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Prehospital tracheal intubation has demonstrated a clear mortality benefit over rapid transport regardless of transport time or expertise

statements.label: B
statements.text: SpO2 should be maintained ≥95% to prevent secondary hypoxic brain injury

statements.label: C
statements.text: Routine prophylactic hyperventilation targeting PaCO2 28–32 mmHg is recommended in all ventilated TBI patients

statements.label: D
statements.text: Brief hyperventilation is acceptable as a temporising measure when transtentorial herniation is imminent

questions.explanation: Prehospital intubation evidence is elusive — the priority is preventing hypoxia and hypotension, not a specific airway strategy. SpO2 ≥95% prevents secondary hypoxic injury. Routine prophylactic hyperventilation is contraindicated (risks ischaemia). Brief hyperventilation is reserved for crisis management before surgery.

questions.question: Regarding prevention of secondary brain injury in the early TBI phase, indicate whether each statement is TRUE or FALSE.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A single episode of systolic BP <90 mmHg is associated with significantly worse neurological outcome after severe TBI

statements.label: B
statements.text: Maintaining PaCO2 >45 mmHg is safe in ventilated TBI patients as hypercapnia does not affect intracranial dynamics

statements.label: C
statements.text: Hyperthermia must be actively treated in TBI patients as it worsens secondary brain injury

statements.label: D
statements.text: A blood glucose target of 4–6 mmol/L is recommended in severe TBI to minimise cerebral excitotoxicity

questions.explanation: Even a single hypotensive episode significantly worsens TBI mortality. Hypercapnia causes cerebral vasodilation, raising ICP — NOT safe. Hyperthermia increases cerebral metabolic demand and ICP and must be treated. Tight glycaemic control (4–6 mmol/L) risks cerebral glucose depletion; the recommended TBI target is approximately 8.3–11 mmol/L.

questions.section: TBI Part II: Secondary Brain Injury
questions.question: A 45-year-old is brought to the emergency department following a high-speed road traffic collision. The image shows a finding noted during physical examination. What does this clinical sign most strongly suggest?
questions.explanation: The image shows ecchymosis over the mastoid process (Battle's sign), a delayed indicator of basal skull fracture. It typically appears 24–48 hours post-injury as blood tracks along fascial planes. Other signs include periorbital ecchymosis (raccoon eyes), haemotympanum, and CSF otorrhoea/rhinorrhoea. Its presence guides management but does not independently mandate surgery.

questions.section: TBI Part II: Secondary Brain Injury
questions.question: On non-contrast CT, a hyperdense biconvex collection is seen at the right temporal convexity, tightly bounded by the coronal and squamous suture lines, with 9 mm of midline shift. Which diagnosis is MOST consistent?
questions.explanation: Epidural haematomas (EDH) present as biconvex (lens-shaped) hyperdense collections bounded by suture lines, where the dura is tightly adherent. EDH most commonly results from middle meningeal artery laceration after temporal bone fracture and classically presents with a lucid interval followed by deterioration. Acute SDH is crescent-shaped and can cross suture lines.

questions.section: TBI Part II: Secondary Brain Injury
questions.question: A 35-year-old male presents following a road traffic collision. He had a brief lucid interval and has now deteriorated to GCS 8. The CT scan is shown. What is the MOST appropriate immediate management?
options: MRI brain for further lesion characterisation
Repeat CT in 6 hours to assess interval change
IV mannitol 1 g/kg and close observation
Diagnostic lumbar puncture to exclude meningitis
Urgent neurosurgical referral for haematoma evacuation
questions.explanation: The CT shows a large hyperdense acute intracranial haematoma with significant mass effect — a neurosurgical emergency. The classic lucid interval followed by neurological deterioration indicates an expanding haematoma requiring immediate craniotomy. Mannitol may temporise but must not delay surgery. MRI and LP are contraindicated in this acute setting.

questions.section: TBI Part II: Secondary Brain Injury
questions.question: This CT brain is from a patient following a severe deceleration injury. The pattern of multiple bilateral hyperdense lesions is MOST consistent with which injury mechanism?
options: Diffuse axonal injury from pure rotational forces
Acute subdural haematoma from bridging vein rupture
Bilateral epidural haematomas from temporal fractures
questions.explanation: Multiple bilateral hyperdense lesions represent haemorrhagic contusions at the impact site (coup) and the diametrically opposite surface (contrecoup) from the acceleration-deceleration mechanism. Frontal and temporal poles are classically affected. This pattern is distinct from diffuse axonal injury, which causes microscopic disruption not reliably visible on CT.

questions.section: TBI Part II: Secondary Brain Injury
questions.question: Several days after a severe deceleration crash, MRI is performed in a patient with persistent coma. Comparing CT (left) with two MRI sequences, lesions marked by arrows are clearly visible on gradient echo (GE) but absent or subtle on CT. What injury do these lesions represent?
options: Watershed cerebral infarction in boundary zone territories
Acute epidural haematomas not yet hyperdense on CT
questions.explanation: Gradient echo (GE) and susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) detect haemosiderin from axonal disruption through susceptibility (blooming) artefacts, revealing haemorrhagic traumatic axonal injury (TAI/DAI) invisible on CT. These result from rotational shear forces and preferentially locate at the grey-white matter junction, corpus callosum, and brainstem. FLAIR sequences detect non-haemorrhagic TAI as high signal.

questions.section: TBI Part II: Secondary Brain Injury
questions.question: This CT brain is from a 22-year-old brought in following a shooting incident. He is GCS 6 with bilaterally fixed dilated pupils. What management approach is MOST appropriate?
options: Immediate transfer for MRI to characterise the tract
Burr hole at the entry wound to evacuate haematoma
Urgent neurosurgical referral and broad-spectrum antibiotics
Conservative management awaiting spontaneous pupillary improvement
Diagnostic lumbar puncture to establish baseline CSF pressure
questions.explanation: The CT shows penetrating brain injury with metallic foreign body traversing the brain. Management requires urgent neurosurgical referral and broad-spectrum antibiotics (CNS contamination risk), plus aggressive secondary brain injury prevention and goals-of-care discussion given the severity. MRI is contraindicated with metallic foreign bodies. LP is contraindicated due to raised ICP.

questions.section: TBI Part II: Secondary Brain Injury
questions.question: A soldier sustains traumatic brain injury from an improvised explosive device (IED). The brain injury that results DIRECTLY from the blast overpressurisation wave interacting with brain tissue corresponds to which phase of blast injury?
options: There are no internationally recognised phases of blast injury
questions.explanation: The CDC classifies blast injury into four phases. The primary phase involves direct brain tissue response to the intense overpressurisation impulse. Secondary phase: shrapnel/fragment penetration. Tertiary phase: contact/acceleration forces from blast wind. Quaternary: burns, haemorrhagic shock, chemical injuries. Blast-induced TBI is unique in that primary injury occurs without direct head impact.

questions.section: TBI Part II: Secondary Brain Injury
questions.question: According to the Monro-Kellie doctrine, when an intracranial haematoma expands in a patient with an intact skull, what is the PRIMARY initial compensatory mechanism that buffers the rise in ICP?
options: Cerebral vasoconstriction to reduce cerebral blood volume
Reduction in cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen consumption
Increased CSF absorption across arachnoid granulations
Compression and redistribution of brain parenchyma
CSF displacement from the cranial to the spinal compartment
questions.explanation: The Monro-Kellie doctrine states that total intracranial volume is constant in adults. The primary initial compensation for an expanding haematoma is displacement of CSF from the cranial vault into the spinal subarachnoid space. Secondary compensation involves reduction of cerebral blood volume. When compensatory reserve is exhausted, small volume additions produce exponential ICP rises.

questions.section: TBI Part II: Secondary Brain Injury
questions.question: Regarding CT appearances in traumatic brain injury, indicate whether each statement is TRUE or FALSE.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Epidural haematomas are characteristically crescent-shaped and may cross cranial suture lines

statements.label: B
statements.text: Acute blood appears hyperdense on non-contrast CT due to its high protein content

statements.label: C
statements.text: Cerebral oedema produces a hypodense appearance on CT

statements.label: D
statements.text: Traumatic subarachnoid haemorrhage appears as hyperattenuation in the basal cisterns and sulci

questions.explanation: Epidural haematomas are BICONVEX and bounded by suture lines — crescent-shaped describes subdural haematomas, which can cross sutures. Acute blood is hyperdense due to clotted haemoglobin protein. Oedema is hypodense. Traumatic SAH appears hyperdense (bright white) in the basal cisterns.

questions.section: TBI Part II: Secondary Brain Injury
questions.question: Regarding traumatic axonal injury (TAI/DAI), indicate whether each statement is TRUE or FALSE.

statements.label: A
statements.text: TAI results primarily from rotational acceleration-deceleration forces rather than direct impact

statements.label: B
statements.text: Common TAI locations include the grey-white matter junction, corpus callosum, and dorsal brainstem

statements.label: C
statements.text: Haemorrhagic TAI lesions appear as blooming artefacts on gradient echo (GE) MRI sequences

statements.label: D
statements.text: CT is the most sensitive imaging modality for detecting non-haemorrhagic traumatic axonal injury

questions.explanation: TAI is caused by rotational shear forces. Classical locations: grey-white matter junction (grade I), corpus callosum (grade II), dorsal brainstem (grade III). GE/SWI detects haemorrhagic axonal disruption via susceptibility artefacts. CT is insensitive for non-haemorrhagic TAI — MRI FLAIR/GE detects far more lesions.

questions.section: TBI Part II: Secondary Brain Injury
questions.question: Regarding intracranial pressure physiology and the Monro-Kellie doctrine, indicate whether each statement is TRUE or FALSE.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The ICP waveform amplitude is unrelated to intracranial compliance and has no clinical utility in TBI monitoring

statements.label: B
statements.text: In adults with an intact skull, total intracranial volume (brain, CSF, blood, plus any pathological mass) is constant

statements.label: C
statements.text: Normal intracranial pressure in adults is <25 mmHg

statements.label: D
statements.text: CSF displacement from the cranial vault is the primary initial compensation for an expanding intracranial haematoma

questions.explanation: ICP waveform amplitude IS clinically useful: P2>P1 signals poor intracranial compliance. Normal adult ICP is <15 mmHg — not <25 mmHg. The Monro-Kellie doctrine confirms total intracranial volume is constant. CSF displacement to the spinal subarachnoid space is the first-line compensation for expanding intracranial lesions.

questions.section: TBI Part II: Secondary Brain Injury
questions.question: Regarding MRI in the assessment of traumatic brain injury, indicate whether each statement is TRUE or FALSE.

statements.label: A
statements.text: FLAIR sequences detect non-haemorrhagic TAI as high signal in white matter

statements.label: B
statements.text: MRI with gadolinium is the mandatory first-line imaging investigation in acute severe TBI

statements.label: C
statements.text: Gradient echo (GE) sequences detect haemorrhagic axonal lesions through susceptibility artefacts from haemosiderin

statements.label: D
statements.text: MRI is superior to CT for the acute detection and localisation of epidural haematomas

questions.explanation: FLAIR sensitively detects non-haemorrhagic TAI as white matter high signal. CT is the mandatory first-line modality in acute TBI — faster, safer, widely available. GE/SWI detects haemorrhagic TAI via susceptibility artefacts. For acute EDH, CT is diagnostic and faster; MRI adds no advantage in the acute phase.
